title: What a seed collection records
bodyMd:
A seed bank is often described as a botanical insurance policy: preserve enough viable seeds and a species can be restored after disaster. The description is useful, but it can obscure what a collection actually represents. A species is not a uniform packet of hereditary information. Populations occupying different soils or flowering at different times may carry different combinations of traits, and an apparently generous collection from a single convenient meadow may preserve only a narrow part of that variation. Even the word representative requires a purpose. A collection useful for identifying a species may be inadequate for re-establishing it across several habitats, while a collection suited to one restoration site may not capture traits needed elsewhere. No finite sample can preserve every possible future response. The point is not to demand an impossible completeness, but to avoid treating a species label as evidence that completeness has been achieved. A manager can make sensible compromises only when the compromises remain visible to the people who will later rely on the stored material.

The collection process introduces a second filter. Collectors commonly visit when access is easy and seeds are visibly ripe. Plants that mature early, grow on difficult slopes, or release seeds before the visit may be underrepresented. This is not necessarily negligence. Budgets and weather impose real limits. But a collection label naming a species cannot by itself tell a future researcher whether those limits distorted the sample. Detailed records of collection date, location, and method therefore preserve something that seed counts alone cannot: evidence about what is missing.

Some managers object that record keeping diverts resources from collecting more seeds. The objection assumes that all additions have comparable value. Yet a thousand further seeds from an already well-sampled population may contribute less to a restoration project than a smaller sample from an overlooked population. Records help identify that difference. They also make it possible to interpret failure. If stored seeds grow poorly at a restoration site, researchers need to distinguish deterioration in storage from a mismatch between the sampled population and the receiving habitat.

None of this makes seed banking futile. It changes the unit of preservation from an undifferentiated species name to documented samples of populations. The strongest collection is not simply the one with the largest inventory, but the one whose contents and limitations can be reconstructed. Insurance remains an apt analogy only if the exclusions in the policy are legible.
